extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of philosophy (philosophy of science, metaphysics, epistemology) and educated general readers interested in philosophical method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying an analytic, scientific method to philosophical problems: identify logical forms, separate distinct sub-problems (logical, physical, epistemological), adopt tentative hypotheses, and clarify concepts like reality, independence, matter, and the mental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis and enumeration of logical forms
rubrics_metrics.description: it is concerned with the analysis and enumeration of logical _forms_, i.e. with the kinds of propositions that may occur, with the various types of facts, and with the classification of the constituents of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic provides an inventory of possibilities and a repertory of abstractly tenable hypotheses; investigation of logical forms is central to understanding and framing philosophical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as scientific — piecemeal, tentative, hypothesis-driven
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific philosophy ... will be piecemeal and tentative like other sciences; above all, it will be able to invent hypotheses which, even if they are not wholly true, will yet remain fruitful after the necessary corrections have been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer successive approximations, provisional hypotheses, and partial results that can be used and improved; avoid all-or-nothing system-building that collapses if partly false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence of philosophy: analysis not synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of philosophy as thus conceived is analysis, not synthesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to build complete, unified systems from the outset. 'Divide and conquer'—understand general forms and divide traditional problems into separate, more tractable questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical, physical, and epistemological problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Three entirely distinct problems ... have been confusedly combined: there is a problem of logic, a problem of physics, and a problem of theory of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which level a question belongs to (logical/formal, empirical/physical, or epistemological) and apply the appropriate method to each rather than treating them as a single problem (illustrated by the example of Kant's treatment of space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical problem of geometry: minimal axioms and class-based relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a body of geometrical propositions, it is not difficult to find a minimum statement of the axioms ... in studying a given kind of geometry the pure mathematician is studying a certain class of relations defined by means of certain abstract logical properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat geometrical systems as deductive logical systems definable by axioms or by abstract properties of relations; one studies the whole class of relations satisfying those properties rather than any single instantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical problem of space: construct points from data; avoid assuming points ab initio
rubrics_metrics.description: In the physical study of the geometry of physical space, points must not be assumed _ab initio_ as they are in the logical treatment of geometry, but must be constructed as systems composed of data and hypothetical analogues of data. ... define a physical point as a certain class of those objects which are the ultimate constituents of the physical world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model mathematical entities (points, lines) as constructions based on empirical data plus minimal hypotheses; prefer hypotheses closely analogous to data rather than radically different ontologies; this explains utility of mathematical fictions without treating them as literal physical entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt mathematically simplest assumption when empirically indistinguishable (continuity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the mathematically convenient properties of abstract logical spaces cannot be either known to belong or known not to belong to the space of physics ... there can be no empirical objection to the mathematically simplest assumption, which is that of continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When empirical data cannot distinguish alternatives (e.g., continuity vs. discreteness), prefer the simpler mathematical assumption for theoretical work, while acknowledging the epistemic limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological verdict on geometry: not synthetic a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: To the question, 'How is synthetic _a priori_ knowledge possible?' we can now reply, at any rate so far as geometry is concerned, 'It is not possible,' if 'synthetic' means 'not deducible from logic alone.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that knowledge of geometry is partly logical and partly empirical; reject claims that geometry provides non-empirical synthetic truths independent of logic and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for 'real': persistence and correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two elements ... make up what is felt rather than thought when the word 'reality' is used ... A thing is real if it persists at times when it is not perceived; or again, a thing is real when it is correlated with other things in a way which experience has led us to expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these operational criteria to discuss reality, but note neither is necessary in all senses—the absence of persistence or expected correlations does not automatically remove something from the external/physical domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'independent' relative to causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A is independent of B when B is not an indispensable part of the cause of A. ... owing to this plurality of causal series antecedent to a given event, the notion of _the_ cause becomes indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat independence as relative to a specified causal law or series; because multiple causal descriptions may exist, one must state the causal law according to which independence is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realist/physicalist position on objects of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: I believe that common sense is right in regarding what we see as physical ... but is probably wrong in supposing that it continues to exist when we are no longer looking at it. ... objects of perception are part, and the only empirically knowable part, of the actual subject-matter of physics, and are themselves properly to be called physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a view where perceived objects are physical particulars (momentary) tied to physical laws; physics' propositions can determine perceived objects without presupposing psychology or mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological consequence: some philosophical problems belong to special sciences or are insoluble
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of scientific method in philosophy ... compels us to abandon the hope of solving many of the more ambitious ... problems of traditional philosophy. Some of these it relegates ... to special sciences, others it shows to be such as our capacities are essentially incapable of solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to reassign problems to empirical disciplines or accept limits; focus on problems amenable to division, tentative progress, and agreed principles; cultivate patience and modesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontology of matter: particulars (time-corpuscles) and logical constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The world may be conceived as consisting of a multitude of entities arranged in a certain pattern. The entities which are arranged I shall call 'particulars.' ... Classes or series of particulars ... are what I call logical constructions or symbolic fictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regard ultimate constituents as momentary particulars (time-corpuscles) related in patterns; larger 'things' are constructions (analogous to notes composing a symphony), not ontologically primary persistent substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for distinguishing mental from physical
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerating occurrences which are indubitably mental: believing, doubting, wishing, willing, being pleased or pained, are certainly mental occurrences; so are ... experiences, seeing, hearing, smelling, perceiving generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether an item is mental by whether it has the intrinsic characteristics of beliefs, wishes, volitions, or experiential states; distinguish between a mental occurrence (seeing) and the object seen (which may be physical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Painfulness is a quality of sensation, not of the external object
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man says he has a pain in his great toe, what he means is that he has a sensation associated with his great toe and having the quality of painfulness ... it is not the sensible object in such a case which is painful, but the sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating the experiential quality (painfulness) with the external object; this distinction undermines arguments that sensory qualities must be mental because sensations can become painful.
